You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (very strict!)
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$
        *   Settled $dV \le 0.01\text{ V}$
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and 20 MOhm.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude: $\approx 3.2\text{ V}$.

    *   [c0054] `SSHI_LC_Filter`: $V_{avg}$ ok, $V_{max}$ ok, $t_{up}$ ok, settled ok. **Failing: Ripple (48-74 mV).**
    *   [c0112] `SSHI_SeriesL_Filter`: $V_{avg}$ ok, $V_{max}$ ok, settled ok. **Failing: Ripple (30-41 mV) and Startup S4 (0.153 s).**
    *   [c0018] `SSHI_FullBridge`: **Failing: Ripple (21-92 mV).**
    *   [c0067] `SSHI_PiFilter`: **Failing: Startup (0.15-0.25 s) and Ripple (13-35 mV).**

    The primary failure across almost all high-performing designs is the **ripple (Vpp)**. The ripple target is extremely low (20 mV). The current solutions use SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) to boost the voltage, but the output stage (usually a rectifier + C) isn't filtering the switching pulses sufficiently.

    *   The switching frequency is $2 \times 100\text{ Hz} = 200\text{ Hz}$ (or $2 \times f$).
    *   To reduce ripple, we need a low-pass filter with a lower cutoff frequency or a larger output capacitance. However, larger $C_{out}$ increases startup time ($t_{up}$).
    *   `SSHI_SeriesL_Filter` [c0112] improved ripple significantly compared to `SSHI_LC_Filter` [c0054] (30 mV vs 48 mV) but still exceeds 20 mV. It used two inductors in series (L2, L3) and a capacitor.
    *   `SSHI_PiFilter` [c0067] used a C-L-C filter. It got ripple down to 13 mV on S4 but failed startup and ripple on others.

    The ripple is caused by the discrete pulses of charge delivered to the output capacitor.
    To suppress this:
    1.  Increase $C_{out}$ (but $t_{up}$ will suffer).
    2.  Add a series inductor between the rectifier and $C_{out}$ (forming an LC filter).
    3.  The `SSHI_SeriesL_Filter` already does this: Rectifier $\to$ L2 $\to$ L3 $\to$ $C_{out}$.
    4.  Maybe a Pi-filter (C-L-C) is better, but [c0067] had startup issues. The startup issue was likely due to the large $C_{out}$ and $C_{mid}$ slowing down the initial voltage rise.

    *   Current SSHI designs use:
        *   L1-S1 (inversion switch)
        *   Full bridge (D1-D4)
        *   LC or L-C filter on the output.

    Wait, let's look at the "Full bridge" in the SSHI designs:
    `D1 D pzp n_rect DSCH`
    `D2 D pzn n_rect DSCH`
    `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`
    `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`
    This is a standard full-bridge rectifier where `n_rect` is the positive DC rail.

    If we want to reduce ripple without killing startup:
    *   We need a filter that doesn't block the initial current.
    *   The `SSHI_PiFilter` [c0067] had `C2 C n_rect 0` and `L2 L n_rect out` and `C1 C out 0`. This is a very strong filter, but the $C_2$ might be absorbing too much of the initial charge.

    Let's try a different filter topology: **Symmetric SSHI** or a **Voltage Doubler** approach? No, the open-circuit voltage is already near the target.

    Let's refine the filter. Instead of a Pi-filter (C-L-C) which is slow to start, how about an **L-C filter with a larger C** and a **very small inductor L**?
    Or, better yet, a **multi-stage LC filter** where the first stage is a small L and a small C, and the second stage is another L and C.

    Wait, the ripple in `SSHI_SeriesL_Filter` [c0112] was around 30 mV. It used two inductors in series (L2, L3) and one capacitor (C1). This is effectively one larger inductor.

    What if we use a **C-L-C filter** but make the first capacitor $C_{mid}$ smaller to improve startup, and the output capacitor $C_{out}$ larger?

    Let's try a **modified Pi-filter** with specific focus on startup.
    Actually, looking at the results for `SSHI_PiFilter` [c0067], the ripple on S4 was 13.4 mV (OK!). The failure was startup.
    $t_{up}$ for S4 was 0.248 s (limit 0.15 s).
    If we reduce $C_{mid}$ or $C_{out}$, startup improves.

    Another approach to reduce ripple: **Active Rectification**? Not available (only switches and diodes).
    How about a **Capacitor-based SSHI (SECE)**? The prompt mentions `SECE_Symmetric` was tried.

    Let's try a structure that improves upon `SSHI_SeriesL_Filter` [c0112]:
    L1-S1 (Inverter)
    Full Bridge (D1-D4)
    $\to$ L2 (Filter L) $\to$ n_mid
    $\to$ C2 (Mid C) $\to$ 0
    $\to$ L3 (Filter L) $\to$ out
    $\to$ C1 (Out C) $\to$ 0
    This is a double-stage LC filter. It should suppress ripple very effectively. To ensure startup is fast, we must keep the total capacitance moderate.

    Wait, there is a limit of 16 components.
    Current count for double-LC:
    L1, S1, G1 (3)
    D1, D2, D3, D4 (4)
    L2, C2, L3, C1 (4)
    Dz (1)
    Total: 12 components. Well within limits.

    Let's compare this to `SSHI_PiFilter` [c0067]:
    D1-D4, C2, L2, C1. (7 components)
    It had a C-L-C filter.
    Double-LC (L-C-L-C) is generally better for ripple than C-L-C if the first C is too large.

    Let's propose a **Double-Stage LC Filter SSHI**.

    Wait, looking at `SSHI_SeriesL_Filter` [c0112]:
    It had `L2 L n_rect n_mid` and `L3 L n_mid out` and `C1 C out 0`.
    This is just a larger inductor.
    If we add a capacitor at `n_mid`, we get a proper LC-LC filter.

    Let's try:
    L1, S1, G1 (the SSHI part)
    D1, D2, D3, D4 (Full bridge)
    L2 (from `n_rect` to `n_mid`)
    C2 (from `n_mid` to `0`)
    L3 (from `n_mid` to `out`)
    C1 (from `out` to `0`)
    Dz (zener)

    Check components:
    1. L1
    2. S1
    3. G1 (SYNC)
    4. D1
    5. D2
    6. D3
    7. D4
    8. L2
    9. C2
    10. L3
    11. C1
    12. Dz
    Total: 12 components.

    Rationale:
    The ripple is the main problem. A double LC filter (L2-C2-L3-C1) provides much higher attenuation of the switching frequency than a single LC filter or a Pi filter. By separating the filtering into two stages, we can potentially balance the ripple reduction (higher order filter) with the startup time (by optimizing the values of C1 and C2).

    Wait, I should consider the phase and ton for the SYNC. The optimizer handles that. The connectivity is what matters.

    Is there any other way to reduce ripple?
    The ripple is $V_{pp} \approx \frac{I_{load}}{f \cdot C_{out}}$ for a simple C filter.
    For a load of $R_L = 150\text{ k}\Omega$ (S2) and $V_{out} = 2.2\text{ V}$, $I_{load} \approx 14.6\text{ \mu A}$.
    $V_{pp} = \frac{14.6\text{ \mu A}}{200\text{ Hz} \cdot 2.2\text{ \mu F}} \approx 33\text{ mV}$.
    To get 20 mV, we need $C_{out} \approx 3.6\text{ \mu F}$.
    But $C_{out} = 3.6\text{ \mu F}$ might slow down startup.
    $t_{up} \approx \frac{C \cdot V}{I_{avg}}$.
    For S4 (weak excitation), $I_{avg}$ is very low.
    S4: $I_p = 30\text{ \mu A}$. $I_{avg} \approx \frac{2 I_p}{\pi} \times \text{efficiency} \approx 19\text{ \mu A} \times 0.6 \approx 11\text{ \mu A}$.

    Conclusion: **We CANNOT rely on $C_{out}$ alone to solve the ripple.** An LC filter is absolutely necessary because it reduces the peak current reaching the capacitor and allows the capacitor to be smaller.

    The L-C-L-C filter is a 4th order filter.
    The attenuation is much steeper. This allows $C_{out}$ to be smaller (helping startup) while still achieving low ripple.
